None is a genuine n=0 zero this case could honestly claim as new_coverage -- the concept brief explicitly asked for reinforcement of thin (n=1) skills, not a zero-coverage close, so new_coverage[] is correctly empty here, the same class of finding as the Archery Camp/Curves Turn-Optimal Can reinforcement carve-out on tier1_structural.py's T1-10 (skills/case-readiness/SKILL.md, 2026-08-17). geometry-triangle (n=4, D1's diagram/labeling requirement) and the three advanced-numbers decimal/percent skills in standards[] are supporting operations genuinely forced by D1 and D5, not reinforcement targets themselves -- all already well covered (n=4/39/35/78).

deliverables.text: A dimensioned elevation sketch of each truss option showing every panel point, chord segment, and web triangle, with each triangle's three side lengths labeled.
Apply the Triangle Inequality Theorem to determine whether two salvaged 3.5-ft members can close the web triangle required by each option's panel length; show the inequality check for each.
Classify every one of The Warren Line's web triangles by side length and by angle, using the actual side lengths to explain why they must be acute.
Classify The Low Line's repeating interior web triangle (naming its base and legs) and its one non-repeating end triangle by side length and angle.
A full fabrication takeoff: chord/diagonal steel weight, gusset joint count, total fabricated cost, and cost per foot of span for each option; state the winner and margin.

balance.argument_a: The Warren Line needs only 3 panels (7 gusset joints) and its deeper 6.93-ft truss lets it use lighter L3x3x1/4 chord steel (4.89 lb/ft) -- fewer, cheaper connections and a lighter chord section, even though all 48 ft of diagonal steel must be purchased new since the salvage fails the Triangle Inequality Theorem for an 8-ft panel (3.5+3.5=7<8). Total: $509.21 ($21.22/ft).
balance.argument_b: The Low Line reuses all 8 interior diagonals from the county's already-owned 3.5-ft salvage (3.5+3.5=7>6, a valid triangle with a real 1-ft margin) at zero marginal material cost, cutting new-steel diagonal purchases from 48 ft to just the two 7-ft sway braces (14 ft) -- but its shallower 1.80-ft depth forces heavier L3x3x3/8 chord steel (7.17 lb/ft) across more total chord length, and its 4 panels need 9 gusset joints instead of 7. Total: $597.77 ($24.91/ft) -- material cost is nearly a wash with Option A ($190.34 vs $192.32); the deciding factor is almost entirely the two extra joints' labor.
balance.margin_basis: Total fabricated steel cost (chord steel weight x price/lb + new-purchase diagonal/brace steel weight x price/lb + gusset joint count x labor hours x wage rate) divided by the 24-ft span, computed in cases/creek-span/sensitivity_model.py from Appendices A, D, E and F figures.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Shop labor hours to fabricate and weld one gusset-plate panel-point connection
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public per-connection timing study exists for small pedestrian-truss gusset fabrication (layout, drilling/punching, fitting, and welding one panel point); this is the case author's estimate from how the operation is actually performed in a small structural shop.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The answer is sensitive to this value -- it is the only cost driver that scales directly with The Low Line's extra panel-point count. Flexed +/-50% in Tier 2 probe 5: margin ranges 10.99% (at 0.75 hr/joint) to 16.70% (at 2.25 hr/joint); The Warren Line (A) remains the winner across the full flex range.

sensitivity_note: MA1 (gusset-joint labor hours) is the case's only stated modeling assumption and the only cost driver not fixed by sourced or given data. At the stated 1.5 hr/joint, the base margin is 14.81% favoring The Warren Line (A). Flexing MA1 +/-50% moves the margin between roughly 11% and 17% without changing the winner (see sensitivity_model.py). Appendix D's steel price (S4, MEDIUM confidence, derived from an industry blog's stated range rather than a single named index) is the case's softest *sourced* figure, but because it scales both options' material cost by the same factor it is not independently dilemma-flipping. The Twist in FACILITATOR.md (combining two of The Low Line's panel points into one field connection, dropping its joint count from 9 to 8) narrows the margin to 7.84% without flipping the winner -- the discussion point is how fragile a 14.81% margin built mostly on an unverified labor-hour estimate actually is.
